subtitles.text: Let’s look at the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model.
We place N spins, and connect every single pair of them with a random coupling. Red couplings are positive, blue ones are negative.
Each spin, sigma i, points either up or down.
The energy adds up, over all pairs, the coupling J i j times the two spins.
The couplings are drawn from a Gaussian with mean zero and variance one over N. They’re drawn once, and then frozen.
A positive coupling wants its pair aligned. A negative one wants the pair to point in opposite directions.
And since every spin talks to every other spin, this is the classic mean-field spin glass.
Random signs cause a problem called frustration.
Look at this triangle. Two spins point up, and both positive bonds want the third spin up too.
But the negative bond wants it down. No choice makes every bond happy.
With N spins, there are countless frustrated loops like this, and the energy, plotted over all configurations, becomes rugged.
An enormous number of valleys, separated by high barriers. Cool the system down, and it gets trapped in one of them.
The replica trick.
To get the physics, we need the free energy averaged over the random couplings. That means averaging the logarithm of Z, which is hard.
The trick is to write log Z as this limit, and get to zero, of Z to the n, minus one, over n.
Z to the n is the partition function of n identical copies of the system, called replicas, all sharing the same couplings.
When we average over the couplings, the copies become coupled to each other.
And the natural order parameter is the overlap, q a b. It measures how alike the spin configurations of replicas a and b are.
The first guess is called replica symmetry.
The overlaps form an n by n matrix. Assume every pair of copies is equally alike, so every off-diagonal entry is the same number, q.
Physically, that means there is just one equilibrium state, up to flipping every spin. This was the original solution, found by Sherrington and Kirkpatrick in 1975.
It looks innocent. But at low temperature, it fails.
The entropy at zero temperature comes out negative: minus one over two pi. That’s impossible for Ising spins.
And de Almeida and Thouless showed that this solution is unstable below a critical line.
So the symmetry between replicas has to break.
Giorgio Parisi’s insight was to break the symmetry, step by step. Start from the symmetric matrix, where every overlap is the same.
In one step of breaking, split the replicas into groups. Copies in the same group share a larger overlap, q one. Copies in different groups have a smaller overlap, q zero.
Then repeat inside each group: smaller blocks, with an even larger overlap, q two.
Replica symmetric. One step. Two steps. And so on.
The overlaps grow as the blocks shrink.
Keep nesting infinitely many times, and the overlaps become a continuous function, q of x, with x between zero and one. Parisi proposed this in 1979.
So what does this mean physically?
Below the transition, there isn’t one equilibrium state, but many, organized like a family tree.

Each leaf is a pure state. States that split near the top are very different. Close cousins, splitting lower down, overlap more. That makes the distances ultrametric: in any triangle of states, the two largest sides are equal.
We can see this in the distribution of overlaps, P of q.
Pairs of different states give a continuous spread of overlaps.
And each state overlapping with itself gives a spike, at the Edwards–Anderson value.
Replica symmetry would give only that spike. Breaking the symmetry is what creates the continuous part.
Random couplings plus frustration give many low-energy states.
Replicas let us average over the disorder, with the overlap, q a b, as the order parameter.
The symmetric guess, where all overlaps are equal, fails with a negative entropy.
Parisi broke the symmetry in nested blocks, producing a whole function, q of x.
And the meaning: many pure states, an ultrametric tree, and a non-trivial distribution of overlaps.
Parisi’s formula was later proven rigorously, by Guerra and Talagrand. And in 2021, Parisi shared the Nobel Prize in Physics.
